overview: Fast Use is a bare C03 flooder with no settings: every UpdateEvent, while the player is eating an item that is not a sword, it pushes 35 copies of the no-argument C03PacketPlayer into the send queue. The no-argument constructor serializes a positionless packet with the onGround flag false, so the module emits 35 ground-flag claims with zero movement per tick, roughly 700 packets per second, for the entire duration of the eat. The sword exclusion is a hardcoded guard left from a reported breakage, and the module sends nothing else: no C07 releases, no C08 placements, no look changes.

sections.p: The handler fires on the post UpdateEvent and loops a fixed 35 iterations, each pushing a fresh C03PacketPlayer() through addToSendQueue. The no-argument constructor leaves onGround at its default false and no position fields set, so on the wire each packet is the bare flying variant with only the flag byte. The loop is unconditional apart from the isEating and non-sword gates, with no timer, no randomization, and no throttle, so the emission is a solid wall of packets for the whole eat animation.

A positionless C03 only updates the ground flag; the server keeps the current position. The eat itself completes on the server's fixed 32-tick use timer, which the flood cannot shorten, so the module is a legacy client-side pattern whose real observable is the packet rate and the repeated onGround false claims, not a faster eat. The claims are harmless while standing, since server-side fall damage only accumulates on actual vertical motion, which leaves the rate as the only signal the server can measure.

The held-item check excludes ItemSword with a comment noting it broke for some reason, so blocking with a sword never triggers the flood. The module registers as Fast Use under the player category with no key binding and no settings, and its whole footprint is the C03 stream; the item-use checks that exist for fast-eat and noslow modules key on C07 releases or C08 placements, which this module never sends.

files.label: FastUse.java
files.explanation: The module file is the entire flood: one UpdateEvent handler, one guard, one loop. The isEating check plus the non-sword exclusion gate a fixed 35-iteration loop that pushes no-argument C03PacketPlayer instances into the send queue. The custom constructor takes name, key and category because the module registers with the display name Fast Use under the player category, and there are no settings, no timer, and no randomization anywhere in the file.

files.label: C03PacketPlayer.java (wire format)
files.explanation: The fork's C03PacketPlayer is the wire format the flood relies on. The no-argument constructor leaves onGround false and all position and rotation fields unset, so a fresh instance serializes as a positionless flying packet with only the flag byte; readPacketData shows the flag is the sole field on the wire. This is what makes the module's 35 packets per tick a pure rate signal: nothing in them moves the player, rotates the view, or touches item state.

countering.label: MorePackets (movement packet rate)
countering.explanation:
MorePackets counts every processed C03-family packet, content-blind, and the flood blows both of its limits open. The window accumulator runs at 22 packets per second with an ideal of 20 over 500ms buckets, and the module delivers roughly 700 per second while eating, so the window score saturates on the first tick and the cancel tier (vl above 2 under the default actions) fires immediately. The half-second burst path (15 packets, with 10 as a direct-violation threshold) is exceeded by the first 35-packet tick regardless of the window state.

Because the check scores every packet including positionless ones, the module cannot shed the rate by keeping the packets empty; each of the 35 copies is processed and counted. The lag adaption does not help either, since the flood is sustained for the entire eat duration and re-arms on every new eat. This is the module's primary exposure, and on any server with MorePackets active the module is effectively a self-kick.

countering.label: Timer (per-packet time balance)
countering.explanation:
Grim's Timer check maintains a 50ms balance per movement packet against real time, anchored to the transaction stream: the clock reference refreshes only after a movement followed by a PONG or window confirmation, and the allowed drift defaults to 120ms. The module's 35 packets in a single tick consume 35 times 50ms of balance in one frame, so the balance goes deeply negative on the first eat tick and flags within one or two ticks of enabling, independent of any average-rate reasoning.

The one-directional design (slow movement drains the balance in the lenient direction) does not apply here, because the flood is a burst, not a slowdown. Each new eat re-arms the burst, so the check keeps flagging for as long as the module is on. Between the rate window and the time balance, the module has no way to present the flood as legitimate traffic.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (silent envelope)
countering.explanation:
SurvivalFly is the honest boundary in this set: the flood never moves the player, and the envelope cannot score what it cannot measure. The check rebuilds allowed horizontal and vertical distances from the physics model and compares them with the actual position deltas; a positionless packet has a zero delta, so the offset stays zero and no violation accrues. The ground-flag claims are read against the block cache, and a false onGround claim while standing still on a block is not a fall, so even the vertical path stays quiet.

The value of the entry is negative space: it explains why the module reads as standing still to every physics check and why the only pressure comes from the rate and time ledger. A fast-eat variant that added position-bearing C04s (the TPAura pattern) would immediately light up this envelope instead, which is the standard escalation for this family of floods.

countering.label: UseItemAdapter (release-gap ledger)
countering.explanation:
UseItemAdapter is the NCP item-use counter that a genuine fast-use stream would face: it timestamps C07 RELEASE_USE_ITEM packets and marks the player as hacking the release interval (isHackingRI) when releases arrive under the 70ms timeBetweenRL, which then feeds SurvivalFly's noslowpacket penalty on the next move. The module sends no C07 releases at all, so the ledger never arms and the noslow penalty never fires; the check is a real counter to fast-eat and noslow modules that emit releases, not to a bare C03 flood.

This entry is the gap that matters for the analysis: it pins down exactly which wire signals the module does not produce and which checks those signals would trigger. The eat cycle here is client-animated only, so the release stream that fast-eat cheats rely on is absent by construction, and the module's only engagement with the item-use layer is the fact that it runs while eating.
